oil.summary: Oil markets delivered a split verdict on Friday. WTI fell 1.46% to $91.51/bbl, dragged lower by reports of an EU-led emergency stockpile release and a subsequent G7 agreement to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel stocks over four months. A temporary US easing of Russian oil sanctions added further downside pressure. RBOB gasoline shed 2.40% and heating oil collapsed 3.49% on the day. Brent managed a slim 0.23% gain to $102.56, while physical Dated Brent surging above $120 signals acute tightness in spot markets. The underlying geopolitical bid remains intact: Iran's Hormuz standoff persists, the US deployed Patriot batteries to protect Saudi and Qatari infrastructure, and CME options assign a 77% probability to an OPEC production cut at the next meeting.
drivers: G7 agreement to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency stocks and US temporary easing of Russia sanctions pressured futures prices lower
Acute physical market tightness with Dated Brent above $120 and European diesel inventories stressed, underpinned by Russia's diesel supply embargo until sanctions are lifted
Ongoing Hormuz standoff and US military deployments to protect Gulf energy infrastructure sustain a geopolitical risk premium

gas.summary: Natural gas markets diverged sharply by geography on Friday. TTF surged 3.47% to 76.5 €/MWh, extending a 6.15% weekly gain as Hormuz shipping disruptions continue to constrain Qatari LNG flows into Europe. JERA's CEO warned that LNG prices have further to climb, citing no near-term resolution to the Hormuz bottleneck; September saw 21 LNG cargoes exit the strait, the highest since the Iran war began but still well below pre-conflict norms. European utilities are reportedly returning to coal in response to the punishing gas bill. Henry Hub rose a more modest 1.92% to $3.024/MMBtu, capped in part by a Baker Hughes rig count that showed US drilling activity edging lower. Alaska LNG economics remain questioned, with costs potentially more than double Gulf Coast projects.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz disruptions limiting Qatari LNG shipments are driving TTF sharply higher, with JERA warning of further price appreciation
European utilities reverting to coal as high gas prices persist ahead of winter, highlighting structural demand-supply tension in European gas markets
Henry Hub gains are restrained by a declining US rig count and domestic supply dynamics decoupled from the Middle East crisis

power.summary: Power and carbon markets received limited direct headline flow today, leaving price action as the primary guide. EU carbon EUAs slipped 0.89% to $80.225/EUA, extending a 2.71% weekly decline, even as TTF gas surged 3.47% to 76.5 €/MWh on the day. The divergence is notable: rising gas prices typically support carbon prices via gas-to-coal switching, and headlines confirm European utilities are indeed returning to coal, which would ordinarily lift EUA demand. The month-on-month carbon gain of just 0.54% suggests the market may be digesting the broader macro uncertainty. Physical tightness in oil and diesel markets, flagged by Dated Brent above $120 and the G7 emergency stock release, adds to the complex backdrop. News flow specifically on power assets and carbon trading was thin today.
drivers: TTF surging 3.47% on the day increases gas-fired generation costs, pushing European utilities back toward coal and implying higher future EUA demand
EUAs fell 0.89% despite the bullish gas backdrop, suggesting macro risk-off or supply-side factors are currently outweighing the fuel-switching carbon impulse
Persistent Hormuz disruptions and Russian diesel embargo maintain an elevated energy cost environment that underpins structural pressure on European power markets
